description.summary: A collaborative online horror-fiction project, begun on 4chan's /x/ board in 2007 and given its own wiki in 2008, in which thousands of authors document a fictional 'Foundation' that secures, contains, and protects anomalous objects and entities. All content is published under CC BY-SA.
description.full: The SCP Foundation is a collaborative writing project hosted at scp-wiki.wikidot.com (the SCP Wiki). Within its shared fiction, the Foundation is a secret international organisation that 'secures, contains, and protects' anomalous objects, entities, locations and phenomena that violate normal physical or biological laws, in order to prevent societal disruption. The project began on 22 June 2007 when an anonymous 4chan /x/ user later identified as Wesley 'Moto42' Williams posted SCP-173, an immobile concrete sculpture (referencing a real artwork by Izumi Kato) that kills any unobserved person within line-of-sight. Other anonymous writers responded with further faux-clinical containment files in the same format, and the corpus was migrated to its own EditThis wiki in early 2008 and then to the dedicated SCP Wiki on Wikidot in July 2008. The project has grown into one of the largest extant works of collaborative fiction, with the main SCP series now exceeding 9,000 numbered articles plus thousands of 'Tales' and translated branches in dozens of languages. SCPs are sorted by 'Object Class' (Safe, Euclid, Keter, Thaumiel, Apollyon, Neutralized, etc.) and by individual style; articles are formatted as redacted internal documents. All content is licensed CC BY-SA, which has enabled extensive video-game (SCP – Containment Breach, SCP: Secret Laboratory, Control), animation, tabletop and merchandise spin-offs. The project is widely studied as a paradigm of collaborative internet folklore.

features.description: Articles are written as internal containment files: 'Item #', 'Object Class', 'Special Containment Procedures', 'Description', often with redactions ([DATA EXPUNGED], ████)

SCPs are graded by containment difficulty: Safe (easily contained), Euclid (unpredictable), Keter (extremely difficult), Thaumiel (used to contain other SCPs), Apollyon (impossible to contain), Neutralized (no longer anomalous)
All content is licensed Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike, enabling adaptations, translations and derivative works
The main 'SCP series' is divided into numbered ranges (SCP-001 to SCP-999, SCP-1000 to SCP-1999, etc.); over 9,000 articles existed by 2025

physical.morphology: A collaboratively authored shared fictional universe. The Foundation itself is an in-fiction organisation, but the phenomenon's primary 'morphology' is bibliographic: a wiki of hyperlinked containment files, Tales, and Canons.

abilities.description: The wiki's voting and rewrite system curates an internally consistent shared world from thousands of authors

Independent SCP wikis exist in Russian, Korean, Japanese, Chinese, French, German, Spanish, Polish, Portuguese, Italian, Thai, Vietnamese, Czech, Indonesian, Ukrainian, etc., each with their own local SCPs

patterns: Continuous publication of new SCP articles, Tales and Canons
Periodic contests (e.g. SCP-001 'Proposal' contests) and collaborative events
Spin-off games, animations, tabletop modules and merchandise

range.description: Global internet phenomenon. The English SCP Wiki is the primary site; substantial translation branches exist in Russian, Korean, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, German, Polish, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Thai, Czech, Vietnamese, Ukrainian and other languages.
regions: Major translation branches across East Asia, Europe and the Americas

Sustained high-tempo growth, multiple feature-film and series adaptations, and exponential translation activity

origins.cultural_roots: Late-2000s creepypasta and 4chan /x/ horror culture, with formal influence from RPG sourcebooks, faux-redacted military or scientific documents, and Borgesian encyclopaedic fiction.
origins.earliest_accounts: SCP-173 was posted anonymously on 4chan /x/ on 22 June 2007 by 'Moto42' (later identified as Wesley Williams). The post used a photograph of Izumi Kato's 2004 sculpture 'Untitled (2004)' without credit; the image was eventually replaced on the wiki for licensing reasons.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to creepypasta (as a parent genre), to Slender Man (a contemporary collaborative legend), and to later projects (the Backrooms, the RPC Authority, and the SCP-translation branches that have generated their own folkloric subgenres).

history.modern_era: By the mid-2020s the SCP Foundation is one of the largest collaborative writing projects in human history. It has spawned video games, animated series, novels, tabletop modules, university theses on collaborative authorship, and a thriving translation diaspora; its CC BY-SA licensing makes it a key case study for open-content fiction.

documentary.name: SCP-173 original /x/ post
documentary.description: The original anonymous post on 4chan's /x/ board describing 'Item #: SCP-173' with the photograph of Izumi Kato's sculpture.
documentary.analysis: Independently archived; identified as the founding post by SCP Wiki historians and by Wikipedia.

documentary.name: SCP Wiki (scp-wiki.wikidot.com)

scientific.name: Collaborative folklore / shared-world fiction
scientific.description: The SCP Foundation is studied as a paradigm of large-scale collaborative folklore enabled by Creative Commons licensing, distributed authorship, and wiki-based curation; its growth and mythopoetic structure have been analysed by scholars of digital folklore and game studies.
proponents: Lynne McNeill (Utah State University, digital folklore)

skeptical.name: Fictional from the outset
skeptical.description: Unlike many creepypastas, the SCP Foundation has never been seriously claimed to be anything but fiction. Its skeptical analysis is therefore primarily literary and folkloric rather than evidential.

stories: SCP-3008 — 'A Perfectly Normal, Regular Old IKEA'
folklore.beliefs: Treated by participants and audiences as fiction rather than reportage; the appeal is literary, not evidentiary.

literature: Numerous SCP-derived novels, anthologies and audiobook narrations
